# METHODOLOGY

This chapter explains how the study answers its research questions. It describes how the posts are collected and annotated, how the models are trained and compared, and how the benchmarking system and the prototype web application are built and tested.

## Research Methodology

This study follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) of Peffers et al. [-@peffers2007design]. DSRM is a methodology for design science research, which creates and evaluates artifacts intended to solve identified problems [@peffers2007design]. The study uses DSRM because its main contribution is an artifact, a multi-task model that performs humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. It also contributes a second artifact, a Taglish typhoon dataset annotated for both tasks, on which the model is trained.

The study carries out the six activities of DSRM in order [@peffers2007design]. The first two activities, identifying the problem and defining the objectives of a solution, take place in Chapter 1. During design and development, the study builds the dataset and designs the multi-task model. It then uses the validation set to select one of 13 multi-task optimizers, and the model trained with this optimizer becomes the final model. During demonstration, the study uses the final model in a prototype web application that performs humanitarian classification and NER on posts. During evaluation, the study compares the final model with two single-task models, one for each task, on the test set. It also measures the agreement between the annotators to evaluate the dataset. During communication, the study reports its results in this thesis and releases the final model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset.

## Subjects of the Study

The subjects of this study are the dataset that it builds and the models that it trains. The dataset consists of approximately 2,500 Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. The posts about each tropical cyclone come from its collection window, which runs from one day before to three days after the period the tropical cyclone spent within the Philippine Area of Responsibility, based on the dates in the tropical cyclone preliminary reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. Each post is annotated for both tasks, with one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid] for humanitarian classification and with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner] for NER.

The study trains 15 models, two single-task models and 13 multi-task models, all of which start from the same pretrained transformer encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M [@aisingapore2026sealion]. The encoder has 22 layers and represents each token with 768 numbers. In each multi-task model, the two tasks share the encoder, and each task has its own task head (@fig-artifact). As in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], the task head for classification joins the output for the first token with the mean output over all tokens and maps them to the ten categories with one linear layer. The task head for NER maps the output for each token to the 21 BIO labels with one linear layer, and only the first token of each word carries an NER label. Each single-task model uses the same encoder with only the task head of its own task. Every model is trained five times, each time with a different random seed.

Both task heads are trained with the cross-entropy loss, as in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. This loss is low when the model gives a high probability to the true label. For a batch of $B$ posts,
$$\mathcal{L}_1 = -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} \log \hat{y}_{i,c_i}, \qquad \mathcal{L}_2 = -\frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{(i,k) \in K} \log \hat{y}_{i,k,\ell_{ik}}$$
where $\hat{y}_{i,c_i}$ is the probability that the model gives to the true category $c_i$ of post $i$, $K$ is the set of labeled tokens in the batch, and $\hat{y}_{i,k,\ell_{ik}}$ is the probability given to the true BIO label $\ell_{ik}$ of token $k$. Each single-task model is trained with the loss of its own task alone.

The 13 multi-task models share this architecture and these losses and differ only in the multi-task optimizer that turns the two losses into one update (@tbl-optimizers). The fixed and loss-based optimizers add the losses with task weights $w_1$ and $w_2$, as $\mathcal{L} = w_1 \mathcal{L}_1 + w_2 \mathcal{L}_2$, whereas the gradient-based optimizers use the gradients of the two losses to set the weights or to form the update. Equal weighting sets $w_1 = w_2 = 1$, as in the code of LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl], and linear scalarization sets $w_2 = 1 - w_1$, with $w_1$ chosen during tuning.

The 13 optimizers are chosen by two criteria. First, each optimizer was evaluated in at least two of the seven empirical studies of multi-task optimizers reviewed in Chapter 2, following Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary], who compared well-established optimizers. Second, each optimizer can be trained with the same model and training setup as the others, so that only the optimizer differs. The 13 optimizers in @tbl-optimizers are all those that meet both criteria.

## Sampling Technique

The sampling frame consists of the posts on X that match the search keywords and fall within the collection window of a tropical cyclone. The keywords, listed in Appendix B, are Tagalog words related to tropical cyclones and their effects, such as *bagyo* (tropical cyclone) and *baha* (flood). Where the windows of two tropical cyclones overlap, they are merged so that no post is collected twice.

A post is included when it contains at least one English word and one Tagalog word, with the language of each word identified as English, Tagalog, or other by the dictionary-based method of Herrera et al. [-@herrera2022tweettaglish]. Reposts, quotes, and exact and near-duplicate posts are excluded. Near-duplicates are identified following HumAID [@alam2021humaid]. After links, usernames, and non-ASCII characters are removed, each post is represented by the counts of its words and word pairs, and of any two posts whose counts have a cosine similarity above 0.75, only one is kept.

About 2,500 posts are then drawn for annotation by stratified sampling, with each day of the collection windows contributing posts in proportion to the number of posts on it that match the keywords. The sample size is based on resource constraints [@lakens2022sample], since about 2,500 posts is the most that two annotators can label in 2 to 3 hours a day over the 38 working days from December 2026 to January 2027.

The annotated posts are divided once into a training set (72%), a validation set (14%), and a test set (14%), following the proportions of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. The split is stratified by humanitarian category, so that each category has the same share in all three sets.

## Instruments to Be Used

The agreement between the annotators is measured with Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960coefficient], which compares the humanitarian categories that two annotators assign independently to the same posts,
$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$
where $p_o$ is the proportion of posts on which the annotators agree and $p_e$ is the proportion of agreement expected by chance. It shows how consistently the annotators apply the annotation guidelines in Appendix A. The entity spans are annotated automatically by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner] in zero-shot mode and are not checked by the annotators, so no agreement is measured for them. The categories and the spans together are the labels against which the predictions of every model are scored.

The performance of each model is measured with F1-scores, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. For a humanitarian category or an entity type $c$,
$$P_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FP_c}, \qquad R_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}, \qquad F1_c = \frac{2 P_c R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$
where $P_c$ is precision, $R_c$ is recall, $TP_c$ counts correct predictions of $c$, $FP_c$ counts wrong predictions of $c$, and $FN_c$ counts instances of $c$ that the model missed. Humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, and NER with span-level micro-F1, in which a predicted span is correct only when its boundaries and type both match a labeled span. F1-scores are reported on a scale of 0 to 1, and differences between them in percentage points.

F1-scores are used rather than accuracy, the share of all predictions that are correct, because a model can miss rare categories or the few words that name an entity while its accuracy stays high. In earlier datasets of disaster posts, most posts fall in a few common categories [@alam2021humaid], and most words in a post are not part of an entity. The F1-score, in contrast, is computed only from the true positives, false positives, and false negatives, so each missed or wrong prediction of a category or entity lowers it.

Transfer is measured with the relative change in F1-score from the single-task models, a widely used measure of multi-task performance [@vandenhende2022dense; @gama2026uniform]. For each task $t$, the change $\Delta_t$ is expressed as a percentage of the F1-score of the single-task model, and the overall change $\Delta_{\text{MTL}}$ is its mean over the two tasks,
$$\Delta_t = \frac{F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}}{F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}} \times 100\%, \qquad \Delta_{\text{MTL}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right)$$
where task 1 is humanitarian classification and task 2 is NER. A negative $\Delta_t$ shows negative transfer on task $t$, and a positive $\Delta_t$ shows positive transfer. The single-task score is the mean F1-score over the five runs of the single-task model for that task, since studies of multi-task optimizers measure the change against one single-task result for each task [@navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo].

Training cost is measured with training time and peak memory. Training time is the wall-clock time in seconds of the training steps of a run, and peak memory is the highest graphics processing unit (GPU) memory in mebibytes allocated by PyTorch during a run. The training time and peak memory of a model are their means across the five runs of that model. For the single-task models, training time is the sum for the two models, since both must be trained, and peak memory is the larger of the two, since they are trained one after the other. The overhead of an optimizer on either cost is its extra cost as a percentage of that of equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary; @liu2023famo].

## Procedure of Data Gathering

Posts are collected through the full-archive search of the X API, which charges US\$0.005 for each post it returns [@x2026pricing]. Each collection window is searched with the same query, which contains the keywords and excludes reposts and quotes. Posts are collected and sampled in rounds until about 2,500 posts meet the inclusion criteria, so these posts cost at least US\$12.50.

Users of X keep ownership of their posts but grant X a license to make them available to others [@x2026terms], so consent is not sought from each user. In the collected posts, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and links are replaced with placeholders. The posts are stored only on the laptop used for training, and only the research group and an adjudicator from outside it have access to them, in line with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 [-@philippines2012dataprivacy]. As the developer policy of X requires, posts deleted on X are also deleted from the dataset, and only the post IDs are shared [@x2026devpolicy].

The two annotators annotate the humanitarian category of every post in doccano from December 2026 to January 2027. They are members of the research group who are fluent in Tagalog and English. They first annotate practice batches of 50 posts, collected in the same way but not in the sample, and the guidelines are revised after each batch until Cohen's kappa reaches at least .61, the lower bound of substantial agreement [@landis1977measurement]. The guidelines are then fixed, and the sample is annotated in eight batches of about 310 posts. The annotators settle disagreements by discussion, and those that remain are decided by the adjudicator, who works or does research in disaster management or crisis informatics and signs off on each batch.

The models are trained on the training set with LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl] and the settings in Appendix C, and the settings not listed there follow the defaults of LibMTL. Every model is trained for 10 epochs without early stopping, as in the benchmark of Xin et al. [-@xin2022mtohelp], and the checkpoint of the epoch with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary]. The validation score is the mean of the two F1-scores, or the F1-score of a single-task model, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. The embedding layer of the encoder, which holds most of its parameters, is frozen in every model, and the batch size is 8, because in a pilot run some of the optimizers did not fit in the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop when all layers were trained.

Twelve of the optimizers come from LibMTL, which also provides the training loop, and linear scalarization is written for this study. Where LibMTL allows it, the task gradients are taken at the output of the encoder rather than over all its trained parameters, since this usually costs less [@kurin2022unitary]. GradNorm, MGDA, GradDrop, and IMTL therefore take the task gradients at the output of the encoder, whereas PCGrad, GradVac, CAGrad, and Nash-MTL, which LibMTL supports only over the parameters, take them over all trained parameters of the encoder. In its first epoch, GradNorm in LibMTL adds the two losses with equal weights to record their starting values, and because its task gradients are taken at the output of the encoder, only the task heads are trained in that epoch. The study changes this so that the encoder is also trained in the first epoch, as in the algorithm of @chen2018gradnorm, which updates the whole model from the first step.

To tune the learning rate, each model except linear scalarization is trained once with random seed 0 at the constant learning rates of 1, 3, 5, and 8 × 10^−5^, and the rate with the highest validation score is kept [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Linear scalarization tunes its task weights together with the learning rate [@gama2026uniform]. At each learning rate, the weight of humanitarian classification is set to 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9 and the weight of NER to one minus that value [@xin2022mtohelp], which gives 36 runs.

Each model is then trained in five main runs, with random seeds 1 to 5. Five runs are within the range of two to ten runs used in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@kurin2022unitary; @lin2023libmtl; @royer2023scalarization]. Runs with the same seed see the training set in the same order, whatever the model.

Because a sample size based on resource constraints may not be large enough [@lakens2022sample], each single-task model is also trained on 25%, 50%, and 75% of the training set to draw a learning curve, which shows how the F1-scores change as more training posts are used [@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. Each smaller part is a random subset of the next larger one, stratified by humanitarian category, so that every part keeps the same mix of categories. Each part is trained with seeds 1 to 5 and the learning rate tuned on the full training set. The single-task models are used because each learns one task alone, so the curve shows how many posts each task needs without the effect of an optimizer.

All runs are done with the laptop plugged in, in its Performance mode, and with other programs closed, so that training time is measured under the same conditions in every run. The tuning runs and the main runs are each done in random order, so that changes in the condition of the laptop over time do not favor any optimizer. Because a GPU that slows down lengthens the training time, two kinds of slowdown are checked during each run. The first is overheating, which nvidia-smi reports in two fields, one set by the GPU hardware and one by its driver. The second happens when the GPU memory is nearly full and its driver moves part of the memory of the run to the main memory of the laptop, where the run continues at a lower speed [@nvidia2023sysmem]. This slowdown is detected from the shared GPU memory that Windows reports, which includes the moved memory. Both are recorded every second, and a run is repeated when either field of nvidia-smi shows a slowdown or when the shared GPU memory grows by more than 50 MiB during training, a limit set from the pilot run (Appendix D).

## Statistical Treatment

Only the fourth research question is answered with a statistical test, because the hypotheses of Chapter 1 concern only the comparison of the final model with the single-task models. The other results are described with the mean and sample standard deviation across the five main runs of each model. These are the F1-scores of the single-task models for the first research question, the F1-scores, $\Delta_1$, $\Delta_2$, $\Delta_{\text{MTL}}$, training time, and peak memory of each candidate model for the third, and the training time and peak memory of the final model and the single-task models for the fourth. The comparison of the 13 optimizers is therefore descriptive. A difference between the means of two optimizers is reported as observed in these runs and is not taken to show that one optimizer reduces negative transfer more than the other in general.

The optimizer of the final model is selected on the validation set, so that the test set is used only for the comparison with the single-task models. The final model uses the optimizer whose candidate model has the highest mean $\Delta_{\text{MTL}}$ on the validation set, in the same way as the learning rate of each model is chosen by its validation score. Of the five main runs of the final model, the one with the highest validation score is used in the prototype and in the error analysis.

The hypotheses are tested separately for each task with a two-sided paired t-test on the test set. For each task, the null hypothesis states that the mean F1-score of the final model equals that of the single-task model, and the alternative hypothesis states that the two means differ. Each pair is a run of the final model and the run of the single-task model with the same random seed, which gives five pairs. The null hypothesis is rejected for a task when $p$ is below .05. This level is not adjusted for running two tests, since each test answers its own hypothesis about one task. The mean difference in F1-score is reported as the effect size with its 95% confidence interval. A difference that is not significant is not taken to mean that the two models perform the same, and a result in which the final model performs worse is reported in the same way as one in which it performs better.

The paired t-test assumes normally distributed differences, which is checked with the Shapiro–Wilk test, and any violation is reported as a limitation. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which does not assume normality, is not used, because with only five pairs it cannot give a $p$-value below .05.

## Data Analysis

Because no earlier study reports F1-scores for both tasks on Taglish posts about tropical cyclones, no minimum acceptable F1-score is set. The F1-scores of the final model are instead interpreted through their difference from those of the single-task models.

The learning curve is read at its last step, from 75% to 100% of the training set, following Miranda [-@miranda2023tlunifiedner]. If the mean F1-score on the validation set still rises by more than the standard deviation of the single-task model across its five main runs, the rise is larger than the usual variation between runs. The F1-scores have then not leveled off, more posts would likely improve the models, and this is reported as a limitation. If the F1-score rises by less, 75% of the training set already gives similar F1-scores, so the F1-scores have leveled off and the 2,500 posts are sufficient.

Because no model labels every post correctly, the errors of the final model are analyzed to show which posts it misinterprets and why. The analysis uses the predictions of its prototype run on the test set. The test set is a stratified random part of the sample, and posts that seem likely to cause errors are not added to it on purpose, so the errors reflect the kinds of posts that the model is meant to label rather than only difficult ones. For humanitarian classification, a confusion matrix counts how often each category is mistaken for each other category. For NER, each wrong span is sorted by entity type and by kind of error, which is a missed span, an extra span, or a span with the wrong boundaries or type. The posts with errors are then read together to find what they have in common, such as their length, their mix of Tagalog and English, or their category. In the prototype, the model only suggests the category and the entities of each post, and the staff can correct a wrong label, so an error of the model does not become a final decision.

## Software System Description

The software system of this study has two parts, a benchmarking system that prepares the dataset and trains, selects, and evaluates the models, and a prototype web application that runs the final model.

### System Structure

![System Architecture of the Benchmarking System and the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-1-system-architecture.pdf){#fig-system-architecture}

@fig-system-architecture is read from top to bottom. Its first two phases, data preparation and model training and selection, make up the benchmarking system, and the third phase is the prototype web application. The cylinders are stored data, and the slanted boxes are the input and output of the whole system.

The prototype has three parts, all of which run on the computer of the study, so the posts that the staff of a Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (DRRMO) analyze are not sent to an outside service. The interface, built with React, runs in a web browser and shows the posts, filters, summaries, and forms that the staff use. The server, built with FastAPI in Python, receives the requests from the interface, runs the final model with PyTorch to analyze new posts, and prepares the summaries and reports. The requests that the server accepts, such as a request to analyze a post, are described in an API specification that FastAPI generates in the standard OpenAPI format, and the specification is kept in the GitHub repository with the code. The database, PostgreSQL, stores the posts, their predicted and corrected labels, and their status.

### Use Cases

@fig-use-cases shows the actors of the prototype web application and their use cases. DRRMO staff are the main actor, and X is a secondary actor that supplies posts when the staff collect them directly. The researcher loads the trained model into the prototype and collects the labels that the staff correct. @tbl-usecases groups the use cases into five categories and describes each one and its result.

![Use Case Diagram of the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-2-use-cases.pdf){#fig-use-cases}

| Use Case Category | Use Case | Description | Result |
|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------------|:--------------------|
| Data input | Import posts | Loads a file of collected posts, or collects new posts from X using keywords and a date range set by the staff | The posts are stored in the database, ready to be analyzed |
| Classification and extraction | Analyze posts | Assigns one humanitarian category to each post and marks its entities with the trained multi-task model | Each post has a stored category and stored entity spans |
| Classification and extraction | View analyzed posts | Shows each post with its category and its entities highlighted | The staff see each post with its category and its entities highlighted |
| Classification and extraction | Correct a label | Lets the staff fix a wrong category or entity span | The corrected category or entity span replaces the predicted one and is saved as a correction |
| Monitoring | Filter posts | Shows only the posts of selected categories (such as requests or urgent needs), entity types, or dates | Only the posts that match the selected filters are shown |
| Monitoring | Mark post status | Marks a post as reviewed, forwarded to a response team, or not actionable | The new status of the post is saved |
| Reporting | View summary | Shows the number of posts per category and per location over time | The counts of posts per category and per location are shown over time |
| Reporting | Export report | Saves the filtered posts and summary counts as a file for situation reports | A CSV file of the filtered posts and summary counts is saved |
| Model management | Load trained model | Loads the final model into the prototype | The prototype uses the loaded model for every new analysis |
| Model management | Export corrected labels | Saves the labels corrected by the staff as a file that can be used to train future models | A JSON Lines file of the corrected posts is saved in the same format as the dataset |

## Testing and Evaluation

Testing checks that the software of the study works as designed. The benchmarking system is tested so that its scores and measurements are computed correctly, and the prototype is tested so that each use case works. The models themselves are evaluated as described in Sections 3.6 and 3.7.

Testing moves from the smallest parts of the software to the whole system. Each part of the benchmarking code is tested first, then the whole benchmarking system, then the trained models, and finally the prototype. All tests run on the laptop in @tbl-hardware. The usability of the prototype, its use by DRRMO staff, and its performance on other computers are not tested. The benchmarking code is tested automatically with pytest, so that every test can be run again after any change to the code, and the prototype is tested by hand with written test cases. @tbl-tests summarizes what each test covers and when each test passes.

| Test | Item tested | Method | Pass criterion |
|:----------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| *Benchmarking system* | | | |
| Unit testing | Each part of the benchmarking code | Automated tests on hand-worked examples | Output matches the hand-worked result |
| Integration testing | Benchmarking system with all 15 models | Automated run on a small part of the data | Every model finishes and writes its result file |
| Performance testing | Best runs of the final and single-task models | Batches of 1, 16, and 32 posts | N/A |
| *Prototype* | | | |
| Functional testing | Each of the 10 use cases | Written test cases | Actual result matches the expected result in every test case |

: Test Summary {#tbl-tests tbl-colwidths="[20,28,26,26]"}

Note. The results of the performance testing are only described, so no pass criterion is set.

Before the tuning runs start, each part of the benchmarking code goes through unit testing, in which the part is run with pytest on small examples whose correct output is worked out by hand (Appendix E). The unit tests cover the placement of the NER label of each word on its first token, the scoring code, the 13 multi-task optimizers, the dataset split, and the order in which the training posts are shown. For example, one test checks that PCGrad leaves two task gradients unchanged when they do not conflict [@yu2020pcgrad], and another checks that Nash-MTL changes its task weights during training [@navon2022bargaining], as their original papers describe. Once every part passes, integration testing runs the whole benchmarking system for all 15 models on a small part of the data, from training to the result file of each run, which contains the settings, scores, and measurements of the run. This test passes when every model finishes and writes its result file. When any unit or integration test fails, the code is fixed and all the tests are run again, and the tuning runs start only after every test passes.

After the main runs, the final model and each single-task model go through performance testing, which measures how fast they label posts under different loads, since the prototype may receive one post at a time or a whole file of posts. Each model is tested with its main run that has the highest validation score, which for the final model is its prototype run. Each of these runs labels the test posts in batches of 1, 16, and 32 posts. A batch of 1 represents a single post, and the batches of 16 and 32 are larger than the batch size of 8 used in training. For each batch size, the processing time, which is the mean time taken to label one post, and the peak GPU memory are recorded. The processing time of the single-task models is the sum for the two models, since both must label each post. These results are only described.

Once the prototype is built, functional testing checks each of the 10 use cases in @tbl-usecases with at least one test case. Each test case states an input, the expected result, and the actual result (Appendix F). A use case passes when the actual result matches the expected result in every test case. When a test case fails, the prototype is fixed and every test case of that use case is run again.

@tbl-roles assigns each part of the study, including testing, to a member of the research group.

| Annotation | \[To be assigned\] | Annotation guidelines, batches, and agreement between the annotators |
| Benchmark code | \[To be assigned\] | Training and scoring code, the optimizers, and the unit and integration tests |

: Researcher Roles {#tbl-roles tbl-colwidths="[25,25,50]"}
